newsitem.title: INDIA: Internal polls stir upheaval in India politics.
newsitem.headline: Internal polls stir upheaval in India politics.

text.p: Two internal political party polls have stirred upheaval within the groups which could spell trouble for India's seven-week-old government, analysts said on Sunday.

But the crises within Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party and its vital ally, Congress, were unlikely to threaten his government immediately because neither group was prepared to face fresh general elections, they said.

"I think both parties are going through a process of getting shaken up very badly because neither is used to the process of elections," said Mahesh Rangarajan, a political analyst at the Centre for Contemporary Studies.
India's Election Commission recently announced it would recognise political parties only if they held democratic internal elections to choose new leaders by mid-June.

The announcement came as a rude shock to Congress, India's oldest political party, which has traditionally been steered by charismatic leaders and has held elections only three times over the past 112 years.

Analysts say Congress's 76-year-old president Sitaram Kesri is likely to win Monday's polls, sweeping aside opposition from two younger challengers, who say he is too old to rejuvenate the party that has been hobbled by a series of corruption scandals.
"Congress is an old party trying to restore itself. Kesri is one of the old war horses trying to stay on," B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research told Reuters.
"Certainly, the elections will deliver some amount of shock therapy to the party," he said. The results of the Congress polls are expected on June 12.
The elections have also shaken Gujral's fractious Janata Dal, pitting its president Laloo Prasad Yadav against another leader, Sharad Yadav. The two are not related.
A Delhi court on Saturday postponed the Janata Dal's internal polls until June 16, saying some senior party appointments were fraught with illegalities.
Laloo, who is also chief minister of Bihar state, on Friday sacked four ministers who were prominent supporters of his rival. Two other ministers promptly resigned in solidarity.

"The Janata Dal is in a very serious crisis," Rangarajan said. "What we're seeing is an internal war of attrition, and I wouldn't rule out a split in the party. It is difficult to see how they will manage for another six months.
"Gujral has not been able to establish his authority. You can expect very turbulent waters for the government," he said.

Gujral has already been embarrassed by a federal police decision to prosecute Laloo, as the Indian press calls him, in connection with a $280 million scandal over fodder purchases. Laloo says he is innocent and has resolutely refused to resign.
Verghese said turmoil would eventually subside.
"No one in the Janata Dal sees any advantage in breaking the government, and I think they will all hang together," Verghese said. "At the end of the day, they'll all feel a bit foolish."
The Janata Dal is the largest party within Gujral's 15-party centre-left United Front government, which leans heavily on Congress support in parliament.
Congress, which has ruled India for all but five years since independence from British rule in 1947, toppled Gujral's predecessor by withdrawing its backing in March.
Rangarajan said Congress was unlikely to attempt a repeat. "I don't think it's in a resurgent phase," he added.
The party's infighting rose to the surface only after Sonia Gandhi, the Italian-born widow of Congress former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, decided not to join the race, Rangarajan said.

"I think a huge number of Congressmen were looking around in absolute desperation to see if Sonia could help them," he said. "They're in a very confused state, and until the dust of the election settles, they really don't know what to do.
"Gujral has been very good at managing the equation with Congress," he added. "It's the problems within the Janata Dal that will be a real minefield."
